questions.q: What are the signs of the coordinates of a point lying in the third quadrant?
questions.a: The signs are (−, −). Both x and y coordinates are negative. A wrong answer like (+, −) or (−, +) reveals the student has memorised the quadrant order incorrectly or confuses the x/y sign correspondence. They may be recalling the sequence I(+,+), II(−,+), III(−,−), IV(+,-) but misordering the quadrants (e.g., thinking III is bottom-right).

questions.q: A point has coordinates (−5, 0). In which quadrant does it lie? Explain why.
questions.a: The point (−5, 0) lies on the negative x-axis, not in any quadrant. A quadrant requires both coordinates to be non-zero. If a student says "Quadrant II because x is negative and y is zero", they misunderstand that axes are boundaries between quadrants, not part of them. This misconception often leads to errors in later problems where axis points are excluded from quadrant-based case analysis.

questions.q: Plot the points P(2, −3), Q(−4, −1), R(−2, 5), S(3, 4) on a Cartesian plane. Write the quadrant for each point.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify signs of each point. P(+,−) → Quadrant IV. Q(−,−) → Quadrant III. R(−,+) → Quadrant II. S(+,+) → Quadrant I. Step 2: Verify by mental plotting: P right 2, down 3 → IV; Q left 4, down 1 → III; R left 2, up 5 → II; S right 3, up 4 → I. A wrong answer like placing Q in IV reveals the student ignores the sign of y or confuses left/right with up/down. They may be reading coordinates as (y, x) instead of (x, y).

questions.q: If a point (a, b) lies in Quadrant II, what can you say about the signs of a and b? If the same point is reflected across the y-axis, in which quadrant will its image lie? Justify.
questions.a: In Quadrant II, a < 0 (negative) and b > 0 (positive). Reflection across the y-axis changes the sign of x: image is (−a, b). Since a < 0, −a > 0. So the image has coordinates (+, +) and lies in Quadrant I. A wrong answer like "Quadrant III" reveals the student thinks reflection across y-axis changes both signs, or they confuse reflection across y-axis with reflection across origin. They may not connect the algebraic sign change to the geometric transformation.

questions.q: A student claims: "The point (−3, −4) is in Quadrant IV because both numbers are negative and 4 > 3." Evaluate this statement and correct the error.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. (−3, −4) has both coordinates negative, so it lies in Quadrant III, not IV. The student's reasoning uses the magnitude comparison (4 > 3) which is irrelevant for quadrant determination; only signs matter. The error reveals a misconception that the larger absolute value determines the quadrant, or confusion between Quadrant III (−,−) and Quadrant IV (+,−). They may be misremembering the mnemonic "All Students Take Calculus" (ASTC) for trigonometric signs and misapplying it to coordinates.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (Indian context) where identifying the quadrant of a coordinate is necessary. Define the origin, axes directions, and give coordinates for at least two locations in different quadrants. Explain why quadrant identification matters in your scenario.
questions.a: Example: A drone delivery service in Bengaluru uses a warehouse as origin (0,0). North is +y, East is +x. Location A: a hospital 5 km West, 3 km North → (−5, 3) Quadrant II. Location B: a school 4 km East, 2 km South → (4, −2) Quadrant IV. Quadrant identification matters because the drone's navigation software uses quadrant-specific turning algorithms (e.g., NW vs SE sectors have different no-fly zones). A good answer includes clear origin, axis definitions, coordinates with correct signs, distinct quadrants, and a plausible reason why quadrant matters (routing, regulations, signal sectors). A poor answer uses vague directions, puts both points in same quadrant, or gives a trivial reason like "to know where it is".

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ plane is divided into four quadrants by the x-axis and y-axis.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a ______ agent in Delhi starting at Connaught Place (origin).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly determine the quadrant of any point given its coordinates, state the sign pattern for each quadrant, and explain why the signs follow that pattern based on the direction of the axes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a delivery agent in Delhi starting at ______ Place (origin).
